title: Mistä: answering with -sta and -stä
summary: Mistä asks for a source: where someone comes from or where something is taken from. Mistä sinä tulet? — Tulen koulusta.
objectives: Use mistä to ask for an inside-place source or origin.
Answer where from with a taught -sta or -stä form.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
Plural means more than one in this grammatical pattern.
A stem is the part of a word to which an ending is attached.
The elative is the from-inside form, answering where from.
Mistä asks for a source: where someone comes from or where something is taken from. In the inside-place family, -ssa/-ssä changes to -sta/-stä.
keyPoints: Mistä asks where from, not where or where to.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: Koulusta means from school, not at school. Use the same source form in a short reply or after the provided verb: Tulen koulusta (“I am coming from school”). With kotoisin (“originally from”), the source describes origin rather than today's journey.
A natural short reply to “Mistä sinä tulet?” is “Koulusta.” (“From school.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
A source correction still answers where from. The supplied negative phrase en tule means I am not coming; both place forms keep the source ending.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: Use a source ending -sta/-stä in these inside-place answers.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: koulusta means from school here. Koulu + -sta gives koulusta, indicating the source.
kahvilasta means from the cafe here. Kahvila + -sta gives kahvilasta.
kirjastosta means from the library here. Kirjasto + -sta gives kirjastosta.
metsästä means from the forest here. Metsä + front-vowel -stä gives metsästä.
Suomesta means from Finland here. Suomi uses the stem Suome- with -sta: Suomesta.
Ruotsista means from Sweden here. Ruotsi + -sta gives Ruotsista.
hallista means from the hall here. Halli + -sta gives hallista.
kaupungista means from the city here. Kaupunki changes nk to ng before -sta: kaupungista. The full stem is supplied.
Virosta means from Estonia here. Viro + -sta gives Virosta.
keyPoints: Use a source ending -sta/-stä in these inside-place answers.

steps: Mistä: where from; question asking where from. Mistä is the elative question form and asks for the source.
sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
tulet: you come; verb (the action or state). Use the stem tule- and singular second-person -t: tulet.
Tulen: I come; verb (the action or state). Tulla removes -la and adds e to form tule-, then adds -n: tulen.
koulusta: from school; source. Koulu + -sta gives koulusta, indicating the source.
Mistä: where from; question asking where from. Mistä is the elative question form and asks for the source.
hän: he or she; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Hän refers to one other person without specifying gender.
tulee: comes; verb (the action or state). Use tule- and lengthen the final e: tulee.

examples.english: I am not coming from school. I am coming from the library.
steps: En: I do not; negative verb (marks not and identifies the person). En is the first-person singular negative verb. The main verb takes its negative form.
tule: come; main verb after the negative verb. Remove -n from tulen to obtain the negative main-verb form tule; the negative verb carries the person.
